note: The fetch ledger and the sentence ledger of the gated-briefs package (docs/wave8-contracts.md, section 9). Each brief under infra/intake/briefs/ lists the pages it was written from; every page was fetched with WebFetch in the writing session, and the claims below are the sentences of a brief that restate a source, each with a locator and, for a regulation, a verbatim quote of 25 words or fewer. The remaining documents are page copy: the squeeze, hub and thanks copy module, the two page files and the open abstracts. Each sentence maps to one claim (C-nn), one existing page with a heading (path#heading) or one decision, or is a short control label. tests/unit/wp-63/copy-ledger.test.ts enumerates the sentences from the files that hold them, fails on one with no mapping and on a mapping with no sentence, and runs the claims denylist over all of them. Interface strings built at run time (the depth line under a card) hold a date and a count only and are denylist-scanned by that test.

What each way of paying for early work asks of the company in return
Seven ways to pay for early software work, compared by what each asks of the company: customers, awards, loans, shares, convertible instruments and crowds.
Founders are often shown funding as a menu, with the amount of money on offer as the only column.
This brief reads the same options from the other side and asks what each one requires of the company once the money has arrived.
It covers seven paths: revenue and savings, federal research awards, loans, private sales of shares, convertible instruments, priced rounds and regulated crowdfunding.
For each path it reports what a public source says the mechanism is, then separates that report from analysis of which kind of company the path tends to suit.
It also lists questions to put to any path before committing, and it sets out the limits of what its sources can show.
Those include rules that change, facts specific to your company and every jurisdiction outside the United States.
The brief is general information for founders.
It is not legal, tax or investment advice.
The legal and administrative choices that turn a project into a company, and what each one settles
Seven choices a first-time founder makes when forming a company: legal form, state, tax treatment, founder shares, ownership of the work, name and tax number.
Founders are usually handed a checklist for starting a company, and a checklist makes every item look like a form.
This brief reads each item as a decision and asks what it settles, what it leaves open and what it costs to change later.

It covers the main choices in the order they tend to arise: the legal form, the state of formation, tax treatment, how the founders divide ownership, who owns the code, the company name and the tax number.
For each one it reports what public sources from United States agencies say, then separates that report from analysis.
One choice carries a deadline that starts running when shares are issued, and the brief says why that one should not wait.
It also gives questions to ask a lawyer or an accountant before committing to any of the choices.
The brief names its sources and states the limits of what they can show.
It does not cover other jurisdictions, and it does not say which choice is right for your company.
It is general information for founders.
It is not legal, tax or investment advice.

sentences.text: Six considerations that follow from putting a language model at the core of a product, and what each one settles
Six considerations for founders building on a language model: risk process, attacks, authority, evaluation and law, and what each asks of the design.

A founder who builds on a language model inherits questions that conventional software rarely raises: output that varies, instructions that can arrive from outside, actions taken wrongly and quality that ordinary tests do not settle.
This brief treats security, quality and law as one design problem.
It asks of each decision what the model may do, who decides and how anyone would know it had gone wrong.
It reports what the National Institute of Standards and Technology, OWASP, the European Commission and two model vendors publish on six considerations, and it labels its own analysis as analysis.
One idea recurs.
The model proposes and the surrounding code decides, because the sources describe no way to make a model immune to hostile text.
The brief names no preferred model, vendor or architecture, and it cannot say how any rule applies to your product.
It is general information for founders.
It is not legal, tax or investment advice.
